title: Conjunctive queries: evaluation and static analysis
short: Conjunctive queries: evaluation and static analysis
lead: Evaluation complexity, canonical databases, containment, equivalence and minimisation.

sections.title: Evaluation and data complexity
sections.html:
The decision version of CQ evaluation asks whether a supplied tuple belongs to Q(D). Combined complexity treats both query and database as input. Data complexity fixes the query and varies the database.

CQ evaluation is NP-complete in combined complexity and polynomial-time in data complexity. For a fixed query with v variables, enumerating assignments has an exponent depending on that fixed v; when the query varies, that exponent is no longer constant.

The decision formulation separates match existence from the possible size of the complete result. A large answer still takes time to write, even when the corresponding membership or Boolean problem is tractable.

PDF pp. 1–12

sections.title: Why combined evaluation is NP-complete
sections.html:
NP membership follows by guessing an assignment to query variables and verifying every instantiated atom against D, including the required output tuple. The certificate has polynomial size in the input.

For hardness, the source relates graph three-colourability to a homomorphism into the three-colour complete graph K₃. Query variables represent graph vertices and atoms enforce edges. A match assigns colours while respecting every adjacency constraint.

This proof concerns arbitrary input queries. It does not imply that every particular CQ or structurally restricted CQ is difficult. Later results exploit query structure to obtain tractable classes.

PDF pp. 13–18

sections.title: Static questions and canonical databases
sections.html:
Satisfiability asks whether some database gives a nonempty answer. Containment Q₁ ⊆ Q₂ asks whether Q₁(D) ⊆ Q₂(D) for every D. Equivalence requires both containment directions.

The canonical database D[Q] replaces each query variable with a fresh distinct constant, preserving repeated occurrences and existing constants. Its facts instantiate the query body. The resulting head tuple is an answer to Q on that database.

Consequently positive CQs in this language are satisfiable. Extra constraints, negation or contradictory built-in comparisons would change the assumptions; the satisfiability statement is for the basic language presented here.

PDF pp. 19–25

sections.title: Containment through homomorphisms
sections.html:
A query homomorphism maps body atoms and preserves the ordered head tuple. The containment theorem reverses the apparent direction: Q₁ ⊆ Q₂ iff there is a query homomorphism Q₂ → Q₁.

For the forward proof, evaluate Q₂ on the canonical database of Q₁: containment forces Q₁’s canonical head tuple to appear in Q₂’s result. This match induces the reverse query mapping. For the other direction, compose Q₂ → Q₁ with any match of Q₁ in a database.

Equivalence is checked by mappings both ways; containment and equivalence are NP-complete in general. A comparison on one database cannot establish a property quantified over every database.

PDF pp. 26–31

sections.title: CQ minimisation and cores
sections.html:
Minimisation removes redundant atoms while preserving query equivalence and head variables. To remove atom α, keep the head range-restricted and check for a query homomorphism from the current query into the query without α. The reverse mapping is supplied by inclusion of the remaining body.

Repeat until no atom can be removed. In the source example, R(x,y) is redundant given R(x,b), and R(u,v) is redundant given R(u,c), using y ↦ b and v ↦ c. Mapping the distinguished variable x to constant a is not allowed when it changes the head.

Minimal equivalent CQs are unique up to variable renaming; this minimal structure is the query’s core. Reducing atom count can remove unnecessary joins.

PDF pp. 32–37

quiz.question: To prove Q1 ⊆ Q2 using the homomorphism theorem, which mapping should you seek?
options: Only compare the number of atoms
quiz.explanation: The mapping goes against the direction of containment and must preserve the head and the constants.

source.summary: Lecture 24 studies the complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation, canonical databases, satisfiability, containment and equivalence through homomorphisms, and minimization to a core.

limitations: These theoretical results apply to conjunctive queries under set semantics. They do not automatically apply to SQL bags, NULL values, or additional constraints.
